problem.para: In the body of the Working Draft, there occasionally appears a point that requires particular attention, highlighted thus:
The SQL standard is missing operators on binary data types (BINARY, VARBINARY, BLOB) that allow users to bitwise manipulate values. These operators (with straightforward semantics) are:
Additionally, these operators could be enhanced to support binary integer values as well.
ALternatively, The SQL standard should provide aggregate functions for bit-wise aggregation (AND, OR, and XOR) of binary integer values.
The area of streaming data from sensors has been visible for some time in the market place, but there is no adequate support in SQL. SQL should be extended to support this.

ignores the fact that not every updatable table is necessarily the target of an update. Given an updatable join with two updatable tables, it may be that the SET clause only enumerates columns of one of the tables. In that case, the other table is not updated and should not be included in the list formed in this GR.

It is a Language Opportunity to support a PTF invocation concatenated with a row pattern recognition. The issue is that a can export more than one range variable whereas all existing inputs to row pattern recognition have a single range variable.
should also accept ISO 8601 syntax such as 1985-04-12T10:15:30. See also WG3:W05-013.

In addition to the FLOOR and CEIL functions that perform rounding up or down, respectively, the SQL standard should provide additional functions that round away from or towards zero, or provide what is commonly known as round-to-even.

The provides many options to group a table/multiset of rows. However, at the bottom of all of these options, the grouping is done by columns that must exist in the table. The SQL standard should allow grouping by an expression (similar to how sorting by an expression in an ORDER BY clause is supported).

Specifying USING inside should be optional. The path column is used for the internal computations for detecting cycles, but the user is not necessarily interested in seeing it. Some implementations already make it optional or don’t allow it at all.
CREATE OR REPLACE clauses should be standardized for various schema definition statements, including CREATE VIEW, CREATE TRIGGER, CREATE FUNCTION, CREATE PROCEDURE, CREATE TRANSFORM.

Some SQL-implementations allow the user to specify a FROM clause in an UPDATE statement to specify additional tables that are implicitly joined with the table to be updated and, thus, participate in the selection of rows to be updated as well as provide values with which the columns in those rows can be updated. The SQL standard should provide this functionality as well.

SQL is very good at computing exact results on large sets of data (think aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM, ). This does, however, come at a cost of elapsed time before the result is returned to the user. Sometimes, it is more important for the user to get an approximate result much faster (with the understanding that the approximate result is not the exact result, which would take (much) longer to compute). To that end, the SQL standard should support approximate aggregate functions like approximate COUNT, MEDIAN, PERCENTILE, RANK, and SUM.
The SQL standard could benefit from additional statistical aggregate functions, such as kurtosis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtosis) and skewness (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness).
The SQL standard should consider extending the FLOOR and CEIL functions to timestamp values ( provide rounding/truncation functions for timestamps).

Macros are very popular in general purpose programming languages where a piece of code is defined once and then during the compilation phase used to (textually) replace a reference to it (think #define in C/C++). Similarly, macros can be useful in SQL queries/statements as well. This could be accomplished by extending the existing support for SQL-invoked routines.
Some SQL-implementations support a SELECT without a FROM clause. The SQL standard should consider providing this functionality as well.
Similar to simplifying the JSON query functionality, there is the opportunity to simplify the JSON construction functionality within SQL.
In order to update a JSON value, JSON_TRANSFORM has been provided. JSON_TRANSFORM could be enhances by providing additional operations for, JSON arrays, a merge/upsert capability,

In addition to the s, which (as the name suggests) operate on each item in the sequence of JSON items, the SQL/JSON path language could add methods that operate on the full sequence, aggregate methods.

problem.para: During the discussion of WG3:W22-043 it was agreed that descriptors could be created in either SRs or GRs. However, a better verb that create was desirable and determine was suggested. Some explanatory text, possibly in Framework, is desirable to clarify the terminology and the conditions under which descriptor is to be determined in the SRs or in the GRs. Following, the establishment of the rules, the documents should be brought into line with the new style.

Unicode bidirectional control characters can be mis-used to cause a different query to be displayed than the query that is actually executed. Besides being potentially very confusing for users, this has major security implications (as documented by CVE-2021-42574).
Disallowing the use of bidirectional control characters in comments, character string literals, and identifiers of unicode source text should be considered.

solution.para: See WG3:W23-014 for a possible solution adopted in the context of GQL.

problem.para: Unicode allows the careful crafting of different identifiers that visually look identical (such as homographs) when displayed by interactive tools to a human user. Such visually confusable identifiers may be used as an attack vector and therefore pose a potential cybersecurity risk by hiding the actual logic of a displayed query from a human reviewer. For further information, please consult Unicode Security Considerations (Unicode TR 36).
It should be analyzed to what extent protection against attacks involving visually confusable identifiers can be provided.

problem.para: Support for the Vector type in dynamic SQL should be provided.
Tighter integration of the Vector type and the JSON type could be beneficial.
This encompasses at least two areas:

nlist.item: Vector serialization to and construction from JSON.
Adding vector type to the set of SQL/JSON types.

problem.para: Support for additional metrics, like Jaccard, could be added.
Support for additional vector operations, like coordinate-wise addition, subtraction, multiplication, , could be added.

Passing the vector distance metric as a keyword makes the syntax of this function gratuitously different from normal user-defined functions and introduces a new kind of syntactic construct to the language. Also, users might want to pass the distance metric as a parameter.

solution.para: Either add a separate function for each distance metric, VECTOR_DISTANCE_COSINE (vector 1, vector 2), or make the distance metric an expression of type character string, VECTOR_DISTANCE (vector 1, vector 2, COSINE).

problem.para: FETCH APPROXIMATE applies to all rows returned by from a . However, typical vector index implementations provide approximate querying only per individual index lookup.

The current design leaves it to implementations how approximate querying is to be handled when the rows are sorted by multiple sort items that each are calls to VECTOR_DISTANCE. An implementation is free to apply approximate fetching to the index lookups for any combinations of eligible sort items to reach the target accuracy, with no control by the user. We are worried that this gives too much freedom to implementations and is too unpredictable for the user.
It should be considered how the user could be provided with more control over approximate fetching in the presence of ORDER BY with multiple s involving calls to s.

SQL/JSON value, SQL/JSON item, JSON text, and JSON value are used in the Document. All terms are defined but have (slightly) different meanings. Each use of the terms should be carefully examined to ensure that the correct term is used.
The function descriptions should be standardised
The implementation defined codes for function results should be consolidated.
